title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 Researchers Say Phone Bans Don't Improve Learning -- But They Didn't Study Bans
author: The Digital Delusion
summary: A new Stanford/UPenn working paper on 'school phone bans' is drawing headlines claiming bans do not improve learning -- but The Digital Delusion argues the study never examined an actual ban. The intervention studied was Yondr pouches: lockable sleeves students carry on their person, which reduced phone activity by approximately 17%. A phone in a pouch the student still carries is not equivalent to a phone removed from campus. This follows a 2024 paper that similarly attracted 'bans are ineffective' press coverage despite only studying softer classroom-use policies. The author maintains that the negative effects of digital technology on learning -- craving, fragmented consolidation, energetic depletion -- extend throughout the school day, not just during class, meaning partial measures cannot constitute a genuine test. The paper itself has not been peer reviewed, and its phone-activity measure is inferred from location data rather than direct observation. The author warns that researchers, not just journalists, are now blurring the definitional line between policy and ban -- making it harder to evaluate what genuine, bell-to-bell phone removal would actually produce.
points: * The Stanford/UPenn working paper used Yondr pouches as its 'phone ban' intervention -- but students kept the pouches on their persons throughout the day, and the resulting reduction in phone activity was only about 17%, far short of a genuine ban. * A phone stored in a pouch a student continues carrying is not equivalent to a phone removed from campus -- the distinction matters because the biological and cognitive mechanisms linking phones to disrupted learning operate throughout the school day, not only during class. * The 2024 predecessor paper studied classroom-use 'policies,' not bans, yet generated widespread press coverage claiming bans are ineffective -- and now a 2025 paper by researchers themselves conflates the two terms. * The 2025 paper is a working paper, not peer reviewed; its phone-activity measure is inferred from location-based behavioral data rather than directly observed phone use. * To genuinely test the effect of a phone ban on learning, phones likely need to be removed from the school environment bell-to-bell -- neither paper has studied that condition, yet both have been cited as evidence against bans.
quotes: If you want to test the effect of a true phone ban on learning, phones likely need to be genuinely removed from the school environment bell-to-bell.
A phone stored in a pouch a student continues carrying is not equivalent to a phone removed from campus.
A year ago, the press blurred the distinction between a 'policy' and a 'ban.' Today, researchers themselves appear to have blurred that distinction as well.
This paper does not show that genuine bans fail to improve learning outcomes. In fact, it does not even examine bans in any meaningful sense.
The biological and cognitive mechanisms linked to disrupted learning -- including craving, fragmented consolidation, and energetic depletion -- continue throughout the day.
